turns.text: Our restaurant was like the community's living room. An immigrant entrepreneur on the Lower East Side told me this recently. And from the emotion welling up in her face you would think that the loss occurred last COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 182 week. But her restaurant that she poured her sweat and heart into, it was a cultural hub, closed over three years ago. The business at the time was profitable, successful, but at lease expiration the property owner demanded double the rent. She closed, and the most painful part is that today the space is still vacant. I'm Abigail Elman. I'm the director of planning and development at the Cooper Square Committee, a community development organization in the Lower East Side. We've been a leader on anti- displacement, organizing for over 60 years, and with our coalition partners in United for Small Business NYC we urge you to support Intro 1796. The story of this restaurant, echoed in the stories of the countless stories we're hearing today, it illustrates a widespread problem, and I, I don't think I need to reiterate that the exorbitant cost of rent is the number one pain point we hear, from both long-term and newer small businesses, as well as aspiring entrepreneurs in our neighborhood. So instead of dwelling in the sad news and the heartbreaking stories, I want to offer a hopeful vision. Um, an independent book store owner, who describes her landlords as "my angels", she was displaced from the COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 183 West Village after 15 years and luckily was able to relocate to the East Side, where the property owners, who live in the building, care about the neighborhood, offered her a lease with fair annual escalations. This story of mutually beneficial leases between commercial tenants and landlords, stable, predictable rent increases, should sound familiar. If you read the bill, it's the framework of commercial rent stabilization, and it could be the story for New York City's recovery. There are many good landlords who are already looking at their relationship with commercial tenants in this way and they wouldn't feel much impact from its passing. However, the legislation would regulate the behavior of speculative predatory landlords in the first case I mentioned and in the countless other cases I've witnessed who are doubling and tripling rents, forcing otherwise profitable businesses to close, and leaving our neighborhoods churning with instability or pocked with vacant eyesores. I really love this concept of communifiers, not commodifiers. We need to align the interest of commercial tenants and landlords and we need to pass a strong version of Intro 1796 urgently. Thank you. COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 184

Thank you. Good afternoon, Chair Gjonaj, Council Members Levin and Yeger, and other council members and staff assembled. I'm Andrea Bowen and I'm testifying as government affairs consultant with the New York City Network of Worker Cooperatives, or NYC NOWC. Um, NYC NOWC is the trade association for worker cooperative businesses in the NYC metropolitan region, and I'm here to testify in favor of Intro 1796. Several cooperatives have already testified today as to the importance of commercial rent regulations, speaking from their personal experience and hardships. I want to highlight the importance of worker cooperatives to COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 321 the New York City economy. Um, our cooperatives are businesses owned and managed democratically by people working there and, um, that offers workers greater control of their job conditions and fruits of their labor. The worker owners of worker cooperatives are predominantly from BIPOC communities, predominantly from low-income communities, and predominantly from immigrant communities. Um, while BIPOC people, women, and immigrants are frequently exploited throughout our economy, the worker cooperative structure allows workers, as they are also owners, to determine wages, benefits, and job stability, and this has allowed the worker cooperative sector to be, ah, significantly more stable during the COVID-19 crisis than a lot of other businesses. Um, the council has recognized the importance of worker co- ops by increasing the funding of the City Council initiative that supports co-ops and, ah, the Schedule C. Um, and so we're really grateful for the. Um, individual co-ops and NYC NOWC are all members of the United for Small Business for NYC and support Intro 96 'cause it's incumbent upon our collective power to ensure that rents don't drive out BIPOC and immigrant -led worker owners, um, don't drive them out of COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 322 business. Um, increases in commercial rent threaten the well-being of businesses, but also the social fabric of affordable communities and community institutions like co-ops, social services, and more that have long served affordable communities. Small businesses are a lifeline of the city and USM, USBNYC is a coalition fighting gentrification and displacement of small businesses, um, inclusive of the folks who work for them. Um, it's also worth noting that NYC NOWC and other cooperatives, um, supported Intro 1796 and its municipal policy platform, and that platform is supported by council members Gibson, Levin, and Powers, among other primary election winners, where they'll highly like to be part of the next government in New York City, ah, in various roles. We thank Council Member Gibson for cosponsoring 1796 and look to Council Members Levin and Powers to follow suit. Um, we have an internationally notable system of worker cooperatives here in New York City, but the survival of that system is dependent on neighborhood affordability. And neighborhood affordability is strongly determined by commercial rents. So please keep our worker co- ops and small businesses thriving. The market has COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 323 always required taming and should not be prioritized over the thriving of worker co-ops among the many institutions that determine our community fabrics. Um, and finally, um, I'm a transgender and queer person. Um, I [inaudible] with co-ops because they provide an in for community members who are frequently denied access to economic needs to start and run their own businesses. Um, and I was speaking with Sarah Schulman, who is one of the city's most storied LGBTQ activist of all time about neighborhood affordability and she was talking about how commercial rent regulation is necessary to maintain the affordability of our storied queer [inaudible] enclaves, um, and as go queer enclaves, so go other communities that rely on neighborhood affordability. So, um, thank you for your testimony and, ah, I appreciate your work today.

Hi, everyone. My name is Badr Fuad. I am from the Yemeni American Merchant Association. However, my co-worker, Husam, earlier testified on behalf of the organization, and I'll be testifying on my own personal behalf and also my family. Um, just a little, ah, backstory about my family. Ah, we have been running a bodega, um, in the Bronx for the past 30 years. Um, my family knows the community, um, and everybody in the community also know my family and understands, um, the service that we provide for the community, how, and how important it is. Our bodega have been serving as a COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 166 shelter in a way for the community, provides some sense of convenience, provides some sense of support, whether it's financial, whether it's mental, because everybody is welcome in our, in our bodega and everybody, um, trusts, ah, the fact that they can always rely on the bodega and its owner. However, um, currently our business have been going through a lot as, ah, we have just gone through the pandemic and we're, ah, you know, facing financial hardships paying back the loans and making sure our revenues are back up. In the meantime, our lease was also up and the new lease that we got, um, we were surprised that our rent was increased, um, in an amount that was totally, ah, unbelievable. Due to that fact, my parents have decided to consider moving upstate because they cannot afford to be paying that much of an increase on our rent. Um, this will not only impact my family, but also impact the community that we live in, as we have been providing for the community for the past 30 years. Um, if we don't, please, some sort of rent stabilization, ah, regulations, this will not only affect us, but will affect the entire city as we will be, we will keep pushing immigrants out. Gentrification has been COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 167 changing our city tremendously and this will only, ah, play into the process of easy gentrification through the city. So please consider, um, doing something about this. Please consider saving our community and the diversity of, ah, New York City because rent stabilization is important and it will ensure that, ah, the diversity of our communities and also insure that, ah, communities of color remain, ah, financially supported. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today.
Thank you, and we appreciate it as well.

Good afternoon, and thank you, Chair Gjonaj, Council Member Levin, and all present here today for your time as well as for your sincere commitment to hearing all of our voices. We do appreciate it. My name is Carina Kaufman-Gutierrez. I am the deputy director at the Street Vendor Project, American Justice Center, um, and we're here today in coalition with the United for Small Business organization to say that New York City needs commercial rent stabilization. The rising cost of rent impacts commercial tenants across New York City. The communities that tends to be the hardest hit are communities of color and communities facing gentrification. And this high cost of rent not only makes it difficult for helpful entrepreneurs, many of whom are from the same communities to open a brick COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 176 and motor space, but it too often is forcing brick and mortar store owners to close their shops. I'm gonna share a story today of one vendor who is a member of the Street Vendor Project, Ismael Suarez. He's a former storefront owner who ran a shop in the Bronx for years. When COVID-19 hit he had to close his store because he could not afford to pay the rent, and then when he tried to renew his lease his landlord tried to raise his rent far beyond what he could pay, knowing that this would kick him out. But he was left with no job, no way to make money, and a store full of inventory, and he had to become a street vendor to provide for his family during, and learn a new profession during the course of a global pandemic. Now he is trying to sell off the remaining inventory of luggage that he had had in his store, falling further into debt as he acquires fines because he's unable to get a license to vendor. This devastating cycle of hurting rather than supporting our smallest businesses and entrepreneurs needs to end. New York City has the chance to do right by Ismael, who is exactly the type of person, exactly the type of New Yorker, that our city tends to say they want to support, right? Immigrant New Yorkers COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 177 who have started their own businesses, migrated to the United States, choosing, choosing our beloved city to set roots down in, and achieve the American dream, but are being forced to close by out-of- control rents. We need commercial rent stabilization in order to end vacancies to protect immigrant New Yorkers and to preserve the culture and economy of our neighborhoods. I want to stress that rent regulation isn't just good for businesses. It's good for the whole neighborhood. Because limited rent increases means that stores are less likely to go out of business. Many smaller landlords are already asking for reasonable rent increases so they won't be hurt by this, right? The only ones who will be impacted by this law are predatory landlords who increase the rent to push out their tenants exactly as what happened to Ismael in the Bronx. Passing commercial rent control now is urgent. Our recovery from COVID depends on...
...stabilizing rent for the small businesses that survive [inaudible] giving us the opportunity to build it better and creating an economy... COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 178

Um, good morning and thank you very much for changing this hearing to a virtual one. My name is Catherine Murcek and I'm a worker-owner at [inaudible] Back Care and Scoliosis Collective, and I'm a member of the New York City COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 236 Network of Worker Cooperatives, also known as NYCNWC. The worker co-op community is really appreciative of your continued support for co-ops and we're now urging you to support Intro 1796 for commercial rent stabilization. Our community of democratic worker- run businesses is small but might, predominantly led by women and people of color, representing communities across all five boroughs and a wide array of industries, from cleaning to catering, manufacturing, media, childcare, and more. Access to affordable commercial space continues to be a major priority for our community. The majority of co-ops in New York City have never even been able to access a brick and mortar space because the costs of rents are just too prohibitive. A fair and just system of commercial rent stabilization would help to level the playing field, making much-needed spaces more attainable, for a more diverse array of small businesses. My co-op, [inaudible], is a beautiful little highly specialized studio based in Chelsea, focusing on therapeutic applications of yoga and with the mission of making yoga accessible to all bodies. My 18 other worker-owners and I have been democratically running the studio together in the COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 237 same space for the last six years, which we spent tens of thousands of dollars building out for very specific needs with yoga rope walls and every kind of prop you can imagine. The new lease we just negotiated fortunately starts at a reduced rate, but gradually increases to market rate over the course of the next 10 years. Unfortunately, that still makes our future uncertain because our business has limited options for growing attendance, because our space is so small. Intro 1796 would really help us out by limiting the amount that our rent can go up to ensure we can stay in our very unique space long term. Another well-loved yoga studio that I used teach at in Flatiron called Yoga Union closed mid pandemic after a decade of operation because they already knew that at the end of their lease the landlord planned to double their rent, which was already around $14,000 a month. These are types of situations that Intro 1796 will help prevent. Anyone who says that regulating commercial rents is bad for the economy, I have to ask, is it good for the economy to close or displace long-standing, well-loved, profitable businesses causing workers to lose their jobs, adding to the blight of vacant storefronts, and making it COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 238 harder for communities to build their own wealth, all in the name of maximizing profits for a few? Does it make sense that businesses are being forced to close while vacant spaces are being hoarded across the city, waiting for the highest bidder? This is what destroys neighborhood character, culture, and vitality. The pandemic is not over. Unregulated rent increases are by far the greatest obstacle our small business community faces. Commercial tenants should not be expected to bear a burden greater than their landlords. Please pass Intro 1796 for commercial rent stabilization for a just recovery. It will help our city thrive long into the future. Thank you.
Thank you so much, it's been an honor.

Hi, I'm Charlotta Janssen, [inaudible] Restaurant Coalition. We're, um, we're about 30 restaurants and all of us have landlord issues and, ah, I don't understand anyone who doesn't realize that landlords are the number one problem for us small business owners. And this is a COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 172 huge bill. This is huge for us. Every realtor boasts about us neighborhood restaurants when they sell real estate. Look up any site and you will find mine. Those same realtors are fighting this desperately needed bill. 1998 I opened Chez Oscar in Fort Greene. Crime was high and we were glad if we even had 10 customers. We had put everything into this business. With our neighbors became Fort Greene's Restaurant Row and felt a great sense of community, helping each other with napkins, tablecloths, soda, and more. Slowly all these pioneers that made Fort Greene vibrant and multicultural have disappeared. None of the original businesses are still there. Each, including me, have a painful eviction story. My team is my family. Oscar's chest, [inaudible] is with me since 1999. My GM, Angelique [inaudible] since 2002. In 2021 I realized my landlord was ripping me off on taxes and water bills. What's new? When confronted, he said that's it, I'll never give you another lease. And when my lease was up he evicted. In Fort Greene I had nothing to show for 18 years of really good business. No equity at all. My landlord sold my kitchen for scrap, collected key money from someone COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 173 else, and had a tenant paying more than double what I did. Most landlords do this. They destroy community for money, making running small businesses, family restaurants, and dining out unaffordable. We restaurants invest hundreds of thousands of dollars to open. When our leases are up we can't take it with us, nor do we have any way to continue in the communities we helped build. Every realtor loves to boast of the diverse restaurants that make communities vibrant and those are the first two evict us. In Bed-Stuy I am the only surviving business on my block because I now own. Many dreams around me are shattered. Now giant debts while landlords have mortgages on pause and wait for the next sufferer to charge key money to and double their rent. Oh, and what about roadside? That's what we fought for and they are gonna cash in on, not them, but they didn't fight for it. Businesses that invest into a place as much as restaurants do from sweat equity to [inaudible] infrastructure need rent stabilization like in France. There a commercial lease is a lease for life, much like one's taxi medallion was. Let's clarify gentrification. There are communifiers and commodifiers. Communifiers invest themselves and do COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 174 their best to give services that improve life in their communities. Commodifiers calculate how little they have to give and how much they can pull out of their community. [inaudible] anti storefronts, overcharge, bring in chain stores. The less they give the more they will be rewarded in this system. We need laws that differentiate between the two. Small businesses...
...[inaudible] invest themselves into...
Commercial rent stabilization works. That's why Paris isn't a ghost town...
...and New York City is.
Thank you, Chair. Can hear you me OK? COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 12

Very good, OK. Ah, thank you very much, Chair Gjonaj. I want to thank you and the speaker for today's hearing on Intro 1796 and allowing me to say a few words at the outset. Um, I introduced this legislation in 2019 in response to the small businesses across the city who said that rent was the biggest challenge that they face in staying business. The numbers bear this out. Between 2007 and 2017 the commercial vacancy rate doubled across New York City. And over the last 18 months the situation has only become more dire. The push to address the small business rent price in New York City is not new, as Chair Gjonaj mentioned. In fact, New York City had commercial rent stabilization in the 1940s and 1950s in direct response to economic instability that the city was facing and the strain put on small businesses. Later in 1986 the City Council introduced legislation to regulate rent for retail spaces, citing similar hardship concerns for small businesses. Now, as our city contends with the long-lasting economic impacts of a global pandemic that hasn't been seen before in our lifetime, we are called to ask ourselves how we are committing to COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 13 change. What legacy will this administration and council leave behind for our small businesses and how will we start forward on a path for a just recovery that puts the well-being of our neighborhoods first and includes the spaces that make them so unique. Local government has the ability to do big things and today's hearing of Intro 1796 shows that. But first I'd like to be clear what this bill does not do. It does not cancel rent and it does not reduce rent. It does not guarantee any business a right to a space. It does not guarantee a right to renewal of a lease. It does not interfere with existing leases or contracts. This is what the bill does. First, Intro 1796 would create a level playing field for businesses by establish a commercial rent guidelines board, much like the residential rent guidelines board, that will annually set the maximum percentage that rents for smaller commercial spaces can be increased. It will not be a decrease. There will be a setting the maximum percentage that can be increased from the existing rent paid. The bill applies universally to all commercial spaces under a certain square footage, removing the negative incentive that landlords have to push out local COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 14 businesses and wait for the highest bidder, sometimes causing years of vacant storefronts. The interest to displace a local business is taken away because the next tenant would follow the same rental amount. New York City knows how rent stabilization works. It has given millions of households the security and stability that they needed to start a family and to be able to stay in the city. Small businesses deserve that same stability. Rent stabilization gives small businesses a fairer shot. Chain businesses and corporations have had a leg up in our city for years because it is currently in the landlord's fiscal interest to rent to well- capitalized businesses, making it harder for new businesses to get started. This goes against the interest of vibrant sustainable communities. Second, the rent guidelines board will be able to choose each year whether it will set rent increases, rent increase limits by setting one rate for the entire city or by identifying smaller affected areas. The board will be required to factor in things like building operating costs, neighborhood displacement, local economic impact, and vacancy rates, providing flexibility in a tailored approach to different needs COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 15 across the city rather than a one-size-fits-all. The bill also brings us a step closer to standardized leases so that all commercial tenants know what to expect in their rental agreements. I have seen in working on this bill wildly fluctuating leases that have snuck in unexpected costs, sometimes not until years three or four, when a tenant was least expecting it. Clearer leases are especially important coming out of the pandemic when economic instability can lead to desperation and exploitation of those most vulnerable. And so this bill eliminates the addition of pass-alongs in leases. Your total rent will actually be your total rent. New York City has the clear legal authority to enact commercial rent regulation. There is no current state law governing commercial rent and there has not been one in generations. The city has home rule authority to regulate any area of economic life where the state does not have a regulatory scheme in place. That is why this bill is legal. Intro 1796 brings regulation stability for small businesses in a time of so much instability. It creates a system of protection and reasonable rent charge, rent, rent changes, and an end to skyrocketing rent increases COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 16 and deceptive lease renewals. I want to be clear. This bill does not take aim at small landlords who are often already offering lease renewals and new leases with reasonable neighborhood market changes of 5% to 10%. It does take aim at larger corporate property holders that are gouging local businesses and causing significant displacement in our communities. Now is the time to pass this legislation, and as we start to come out of this pandemic we can offer the stability and the long-term planning that businesses have been demanding of us. Other localities are finding ways to tackle the small business rent prices. Seattle passed a law last summer to cap any commercial rent increases in response to the pandemic. When we fight for our small businesses we fight for all of us. We fight for jobs for local residents, for investment in our local economy, and the vibrancy and diversity of our neighborhoods. Our communities depend on local businesses and I'm proud to be able to put them first in this legislation. There are some folks I want to thank for this legislation. Ah, first, Kelly Taylor and Rob Newman, um, who worked on this legislation, ah, going back about three years at this point. COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 17 Louis Holden Brown, Audrey Sun, Bill Drafter, Stephanie Jones, committee counsel. Um, I want to specifically acknowledge Elizabeth Adams, who put countless hours, um, into working through the complexity of this legislation. I just want to thank her, um, very much. Um, and all of the businesses in District 33 who helped inform this legislation, and members of the United for Small Business Coalition, who have also put in countless hours of work and advocacy. With that, I'll turn it back to you, Chair. Thank you very much for the courtesy.

Ah, thank you very much, Chair. Thank you, Commissioner. Um, I appreciate your testimony, um, and, um, and your willingness to engage with us on this topic. Um, I, I want to ask just at the outset here, um, ah, and, and Chair Gjonaj had spoken about this, um, do you hear when you're speak to small businesses out there in the city, do you hear from them that rent burden is one of the first or second top issues that they face?
Would you say it's one of the first or two, one of the first or second, ah, issues that you hear from them?

Um, has, when SBS looks at, does SBS look at the, the impact of what we call gentrification on small businesses, um, in, across the five boroughs? Is that a, is that kind of within the purview of SBS?
And how, how do you see gentrification play out when it comes to small businesses?
Do you see rent- burdened commercial properties as a, as part of what we generally think of as the forces of gentrification?

Sure, I know it's part of a, of a kind of ecosystem of issues, um, but, you know, when I see a neighborhood gentrified, which include parts of my district, include parts of neighborhoods that I have worked in, in my career, neighborhoods like Bushwick, ah, Bed-Stuy, um, parts of my district like Williamsburg and Greenpoint, um, when I see gentrification, um, what I'm seeing often are upward pressure on residential rents, um, especially those that are not regulated, so if a building is new and unregulated or if it's, um, COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 77 greater than or less than six units, or if it's reached a vacancy decontrol and, and is no longer, um, in the rent regulation system, um, so upward pressure on rents for, for residential, that, that creates a rent burden for residential tenants and, um, at the same time we tend to see in neighborhoods like, like those that I just mentioned, um, that commercial businesses are facing a similar, ah, increase in rent, particularly when there are, um, other businesses that are out there that have greater access to capital. You mentioned access to capital before as another big issue that, that, um, small businesses face. So, um, access to capital, do, do you see a direct relationship between access to capital and rent? In other words, if you are a small business that has access to capital can you pay more rent?

Um, you know, and I just, and, and, and data, I mean, you know, data in this discussion is, is generally hard to come back, and in fact going back and looking at, um, research that was done back in the Eighties when we were talking about commercial rent stabilization back then, ah, there was always a challenge of, of, um, of getting, um, objective data that we can all agree on as relevant data, um, and so, you know, in the absence of, of, of really comprehensive data, you know, there are anecdotal, ah, examples that we can look at. So I just looked at, ah, I, I used ACRIS to look at, um, the ownership of properties that, um, in, in a neighborhood, like I used to work on Wyckoff Avenue and Bushwick. Wyckoff Avenue and Bushwick is a very, is, is gentrification on steroids, OK, it's, you know, you see, um, ah, you know, a lot of small businesses closing down and replaced by newer businesses that are, you know, clearly have more access to capital. They're, um, and, and what I've noticed in looking at, um, you know, looking up the ownership of those properties is that, um, very often they're not, you know, long-term owners, they're not mom and pop shops, you know, mom and pop owners. COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 79 They're not, um, what they are, are LLCs, um, and they're real estate investment opportunities for, for people that are in that line of work, real estate investments, and, um, and so when we talk about gentrification as kind of an economic ecosystem, um, what I think we see a lot in outer boroughs, neighborhoods that are facing these pressures, that face it on the residential side, that face it on the commercial side, is that the investors are looking to make a return on their investment. They have a certain, ah, rate of return that they expect in order to, to make good on their investment, and commercial rent on small properties is a big part of making that return on their investment, and if you are faced as a, as an investor who's not a, you know, has a mortgage, has a mortgage and expensive mortgage, has a mortgage that might be securitized, right? We're talking about securitized mortgages when you have to make a return because you have, you have different investors that are involved in securitization, what is there to prevent, what, what do we have in place to prevent the, that type of the, the, to prevent a small business that is been there for a long time, that has an existing lease, that's maybe been there COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 80 for 10 or 20 years, from, from losing out on that space to another business that has greater access to capital, um, that is, and frankly I mean, you know, when we think about an immigrant-owned business is not gonna have the same access to capital often than, than a, than a, than a non-immigrant-owned business and that's just the reality, and so what do we have in place to level the playing field between a small business that may not have access to the capital markets and a small business that does that can, that can frankly pay more in rent to satisfactory a real estate investment and those investors who are, who must make a return on their investment? What do we have in place to level the playing field, 'cause that's what I think of when I think of gentrification.
I mean, I think...

...[inaudible] things we do, I, I can say that, you know, just in terms of like, ah, my office is on Atlantic Avenue and Boerum Hill. I could speak to the black-owned women business that was three doors down from me, kind of came [inaudible] hair stylist who, who had to go and they do, you know, they do it by appointment and they, they're now doing their work, um, you know, out of their homes, um, 'cause they couldn't afford the rent anymore, um, upon a lease renewal. So I mean, it's...
...it is, um, you know, does, does SBS keep track of how many businesses, um, are going, are, are not renewing, are not able to renew their leases, small businesses?
Um...

So, so, we talked, we talked about data, you talked about data, um, in your testimony, um, and, you know, the legislation as proposed, 1796, does require that a commercial rent stabilization board assess data every year in determining whether, what and whether, ah, there would be a, a rent increase in that given year, either on neighborhood by neighborhood basis or, or citywide, and so, you know, there are, these are the, these are the, in the bill, just want to be clear, just so that the public understands what the bill is. It says the board shall establish initial guidelines for commercial rent adjustments by the first of July for the next seating appointment of the last member of the board, meaning once the board is appointed then the next July 1 will start the initial guidelines. Thereafter the board shall establish annual guidelines to be filed in according with Subdivision G of this section. In determining COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 84 whether to adjust rents for commercial spaces subject to the commercial rent stabilization provisions of this chapter in the bill the board shall consider, among other things, and so this is what's laying out, the economic conditions of the commercial real estate industry in the affected area, including such factors as commercial real estate taxes and sewer and water rates, gross operating and maintenance costs, including insurance rates, governmental fees, fuel, and labor costs, costs and availability of financing, including effective rates of interest, and over supply, overall supply of commercial spaces and overall vacancy rates. That's one, and then two, relevant data from the current and projected market values of commercial rentals in the affected area, and three, any other relevant data available to the board. So my question to SBS is are there any other points of data or any other, um, any other, ah, thing, information, that SBS believes should be taken into access when analyzing what, what should be a, a, a, a rental increase for the, the following year. In other words, the bill, the bill addresses the need for data by laying out what data should be sought out 25 COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 85 and acquired and considered. What else, what other point of data would you, ah, recommend?

Ah, Chair, I just have a couple more questions for the commissioner, if I, if I may. Um, ah, Commissioner, is there anything that SBS or the city does to, ah, address pass- throughs to commercial tenants of, of real estate, water and sewer taxes, um, because that is something that we, I, I know for a fact. Very good, OK. Ah, thank you very much, Chair Gjonaj. I want to thank you and the speaker for today's hearing on Intro 1796 and allowing me to say a few words at the outset. The push to address the small business rent price in New York City is not new, as Chair Gjonaj mentioned. In fact, New York City had commercial rent stabilization in the 1940s and 1950s in direct response to economic instability that the city was facing and the strain put on small businesses. It does not cancel rent and it does not reduce rent. It does not guarantee any business a right to a space. It does not guarantee a right to renewal of a lease. It does not interfere with existing leases or contracts. This is what the bill does. First, Intro 1796 would create a level playing field for businesses by establish a commercial rent guidelines board, much like the residential rent guidelines board, that will annually set the maximum percentage that rents for smaller commercial spaces can be increased. It will not be a decrease. There will be a setting the maximum percentage that can be increased from the existing rent paid. The bill applies universally to all commercial spaces under a certain square footage, removing the negative incentive that landlords have to push out local COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 14 businesses and wait for the highest bidder, sometimes causing years of vacant storefronts. The interest to displace a local business is taken away because the next tenant would follow the same rental amount. New York City knows how rent stabilization works. It has given millions of households the security and stability that they needed to start a family and to be able to stay in the city. Small businesses deserve that same stability. Rent stabilization gives small businesses a fairer shot. Chain businesses and corporations have had a leg up in our city for years because it is currently in the landlord's fiscal interest to rent to well- capitalized businesses, making it harder for new businesses to get started. This goes against the interest of vibrant sustainable communities. Second, the rent guidelines board will be able to choose each year whether it will set rent increases, rent increase limits by setting one rate for the entire city or by identifying smaller affected areas. The board will be required to factor in things like building operating costs, neighborhood displacement, local economic impact, and vacancy rates, providing flexibility in a tailored approach to different needs COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 15 across the city rather than a one-size-fits-all. The bill also brings us a step closer to standardized leases so that all commercial tenants know what to expect in their rental agreements. I have seen in working on this bill wildly fluctuating leases that have snuck in unexpected costs, sometimes not until years three or four, when a tenant was least expecting it. Clearer leases are especially important coming out of the pandemic when economic instability can lead to desperation and exploitation of those most vulnerable. And so this bill eliminates the addition of pass-alongs in leases. Your total rent will actually be your total rent. New York City has the clear legal authority to enact commercial rent regulation. There is no current state law governing commercial rent and there has not been one in generations. The city has home rule authority to regulate any area of economic life where the state does not have a regulatory scheme in place. That is why this bill is legal. turns.text: Good afternoon and thank you for the opportunity to speak this afternoon. My name is Alexander Lycoyannis and I'm a member of Rosenberg and Astis, the largest real estate boutique law firm in New York City, where I have represented commercial owners and tenants for almost 20 years. Among other areas of practice, I've expensively litigated in the rent stabilization area, and in connection with that practice I've studied the history of rent regulation in New York City and the legal authority under which rent regulation statutes have been enacted. Based on my research of the relevant issues, I've concluded that New York City cannot unilaterally enact a commercial rent control statute, such as Intro 1796, without authority from state legislation. While New York State is a sovereign government entity, New York City is not. It only has such authority to enact laws, Intro 1796, as is was granted by New York State. Here, the state COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 185 has granted no such authority to the city and therefore Intro 1796 is beyond the power of New York City to enact independently. The best way to understand the issue is to study the history behind residential rent regulation in New York, which many here have mentioned. In 1962 the legislature passed, ah, the state legislature passed a piece of legislation called the Local Emergency Housing Rent Control Act, or LEHRCA, which empowered New York City to adopt and amend local laws or ordinances in respect of the regulation and control of residential rents. Thus enabled by LEHRCA, the City Council enacted the Rent Stabilization Law of 1969 and similarly in 1974 the legislature passed the Emergency Tenant Protection Act, which enabled New York City to declare a housing emergency and expand rent regulation, consistent with the statute. Here, by contrast, the state legislature has not passed an enabling statute [inaudible] which would authorize the city to act on its own. And, in fact, as it's been mentioned several times here today, there was commercial regulation from the 1940s through 1963. That was the Emergency Commercial Space Rent Control Law, but the important thing about that law that I COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 186 think some people here may miss is that that piece of legislation was enacted by the State of New York, not by the City of New York. Even though that law was aimed at regulating commercial rents in New York City, only the state legislature was empowered to do that. And, and I believe, and if you look, a couple years ago at Assembly Bill A-9622, which was introduced in the state legislature, that confirms that the state agrees with my analysis. So while I don't doubt the good intentions and the council members and everyone else's sincere desire to help, my conclusion is the City Council has no authority to enact this legislation. Thank you.

Um, I, just to make, so the record is clear, I, I am also on the, the, ah, New York City Bar's Real Property Law Committee currently, but as, as Paula stated, my opinions are, are not those of, of the committee and, um, I'm speaking in my individual capacity. Um, I, I actually submitted some, ah, written testimony, ah, a couple of days ago which I think more fully addresses, ah, um, Ms. Segal's arguments. Um, with regard to, um, the authority of the state and, and occupying the field, as I indicated in my testimony earlier under the, ah, under the, the commercial rent control statute that was in effect from 1945 to 1963, that was passed by New York State, and New York City, as with other localities, does have home rule powers, absolutely. It has the power to regulate it property affairs in government and it has the authority to, ah, legislate in the area of the health and welfare of its citizens. But what the courts have continually held over the years is that the area of COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 199 rent regulation, ah, does not fall within those, ah, two areas. And moreover, those local home rule powers can only be exercised in areas that are not matters of state concern. And here the, um, the state, from the Forties through the Sixties, um, enacted commercial rent control in New York City, and it, and it continually, I believe it was on a yearly basis, continued to renew those laws, that law, for, um, a number of years, I, I believe 18 years altogether. But as of December 31, 1963, the state legislature allowed that law to expire, and that purposeful expiration, that purposeful decision not to expand rent, or not to extend rent regulation was just as much of a policy choice as enacting it in the first instance. And since December 31, 1963, the New York State Legislature has elected not to have commercial rent regulation in New York State. And as I alluded to further, um, a couple of years ago in the 2019-2020 legislative session of the State Legislature, there was a bill introduced in the Assembly, ah, Bill A-9622, and the purpose, reading from the built, ah, from the text of the, on, on the website is that it relates to allowing municipalities 25 COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 200 the right to enact commercial rent control measures. Thank you. Ah, good morning, Chair Gjonaj and members of the Committee on Small Business. I'm Jonnel Doris, the commissioner of New York City Department of Small Business Services. I'm joined by Bridget Anderson, deputy commissioner for the Department of Sanitation, and for my senior leadership, First Deputy Commissioner Jackie Mallon and Deputy Commissioner Blaise Backer. At SBS we aim to unlock economic potential and create economic security for all New Yorkers, connecting them to quality jobs, building stronger businesses, and fostering thriving neighborhoods across the five boroughs. I'm please to testified today on Intros 2000, 1796, and 2299, and discuss, ah, the work SBS has done to support small businesses in commercial tenancy and during emergencies. I want to begin by acknowledging the terrible losses that New Yorkers and small businesses have faced following the flood COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 33 impact of Hurricane Ida. Lives were lost and businesses have been ruined in its wake. SBS immediately activated our emergency response protocols to aid businesses in assessment and recovery. We have opened nearly 600 individual response cases and are working with businesses to connect them to legal support for the commercial leases, guidance on accessing funding, expeditors to cut red tape, and continue connecting them, ah, with other services. Let us know if you have businesses in your districts and still, that still need our support and help due to Ida. Our number is 888-SBS- 4NYC. At the onset of the pandemic we quickly shifted our work to meet the challenges of the pandemic. SBS created a small business recovery plan designed to jump start the economy in the short term, while laying the groundwork for sustainable small business recovery in the long term. This small business recovery plan, developed in collaboration with business leaders, industry associations, and government partners was based on four strategies to ensure an equitable citywide economic recovery, support business innovation to increase revenue. Secondly, equip entrepreneurs to adapt to lower COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 34 operating costs. Third, foster close collaboration with businesses to cut red tape, and, four, promote equitable economic growth and support diverse businesses of the future. As a result, we launched 37 additional recovery programs, initiatives, and campaigns, fielded over 70,000 calls through our hotline, and hosted over 780 webinars with over 53,000 attendees. We connected over 5000 businesses to more than 156 million enrolled state, local, and federal, ah, philanthropic funding. And from our April 2020, from April 2020 SBS assisted over 4000 businesses to apply, approximately 305 million in PPP loans. We also visited over 100 commercial corridors, reaching thousands of small businesses. During this work our focus has been on supporting the needs of our small businesses in the hardest-hit communities, including minority- and immigrant-owned businesses. Facing the pandemic and now Hurricane Ida, our city's small businesses have dealt, have dealt with challenges that just a few years ago we would have never thought imaginable. My team at SBS has been working nonstop to support the economic engines of our neighborhoods. When our businesses were forced to shut down last year due to no fault of COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 35 their own, SBS created the first grant and loan program in the nation to assist them. We built on these initial programs and developed a robust recovery aid strategy to better focus on high-need businesses. Our existing strategy has three main components. One, targeted, making sure our products are aimed at the businesses and the greatest need. Secondly, outreach, leveraging and funding our community and business partners to carry our message in a linguistically and culturally appropriate manner. Third, technical assistance, providing training, information sessions, ah, webinars and one- on-one counseling services. Examples of this approach are the LMI storefront, ah, loan and the interest rate reduction grant, which were designed for small businesses in low- to moderate-income neighborhoods largely left out of the first round of federal aid. Using census data, we micro targeted neighborhoods and staggered the roll-out of the LMI loan to reach the lowest-income neighborhoods first, allowing them more time to apply, followed by more moderate-income neighborhoods. Our outreach strategy is partner-based, working with our [inaudible] 76, ah, BIDs, and merchant associations to reach COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 36 businesses in their communities. In the neighborhoods that do not benefit from these networks we develop the strategic impact COVID-19 commercial district support grant. This grant focused on hard- to-reach communities and funded neighborhoods, community, neighborhood community groups as trusted partners and messengers of our programs, ah, to businesses in their own languages. This work, ah, complemented our own boots on the ground outreach operations, which consisted of SBS outreach team, the council, ah, supported chamber on the go program, our emergency response unit, and our compliance advisors, all building trust and educating businesses on the available assistance. Lastly, our technical assistance team, ah, accessible online or over the phone, our created weekly and often daily webinars along with one-on-one assistance to help businesses get the funding they needs. To date, 75% of the LMI storefront loan program and 90% of the interest rate reduction grants have gone to minority-owned businesses in those communities. Even with this success, we continue to evaluate our work to determine better strategies to reach business owners. In this vein, we are supportive of Intro 2000, which COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 37 provides transparency and funding distributions during emergency aid relief operations. By tracking and sharing this valuable metric we can evaluate and improve our strategies to continue to make them better. Moving on to Intro 1796 and Intro 2299. New York's small businesses have taken a one-two punch of nearly biblical proportions and we need to provide the necessary relief to ensure, ah, they recovery and thrive. Prior to the pandemic the mayor stated, ah, the time was right to look at whether we can make commercial rent control work and to find ways to continue supporting small businesses while protecting them from excessive rent increases. But reduced foot traffic due to the pandemic and the leap in e- commerce have fundamentally changed commercial real estate markets, with many neighborhoods seeing increased vacancy and reduced rents. Regulations could have unintended consequences that create new barriers, [inaudible] other local entrepreneurs from entering the market and, and starting new retail businesses. Many of the businesses that we work with do not have formal leases and regulations could increase this trend, hurting these businesses in future years. These are some of the reasons why we COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 38 need a comprehensive review of the economic impacts this could have on a range of small businesses and neighborhoods. SBS has always committed to providing the tools businesses need to address their lease and rent challenges, and we've doubled down on those efforts since the onset of COVID-19. We know that the challenges small businesses face with rent uncertainty is often centered around difficulties navigating the leasing processing and ensuring the right provisions are in place. To support them with this, ah, with their lease we provided free legal services through our commercial lease assistance program. Through this initiative our pro bono attorneys help businesses understand, amend, renew, or terminate an existing lease. They also negotiate on behalf of the commercial tenant with their landlord and provide advice and referral services when litigation cannot be avoided. Since its inception, ah, this program has served 925 businesses and this year we increased the budget to 10.4 million dollars to provide more support during this difficult time. We also produced a 40-page commercial leasing guide. The guide covers the entire process of renting a commercial space, including, ah, selecting COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 39 a space, ah, explaining lease terms, and the process of signing, hiring contractors, and lease renewal, and termination process. SBS, ah, complements, ah, this with live commercial lease education workshops for more in-depth education. In closing, I thank you for your efforts and passion on behalf of our city's small businesses. I know that together we can provide support to one of the city's most vital assets. Very good, OK. Ah, thank you very much, Chair Gjonaj. I want to thank you and the speaker for today's hearing on Intro 1796 and allowing me to say a few words at the outset. Um, I introduced this legislation in 2019 in response to the small businesses across the city who said that rent was the biggest challenge that they face in staying business. The numbers bear this out. Between 2007 and 2017 the commercial vacancy rate doubled across New York City. And over the last 18 months the situation has only become more dire. The push to address the small business rent price in New York City is not new, as Chair Gjonaj mentioned. In fact, New York City had commercial rent stabilization in the 1940s and 1950s in direct response to economic instability that the city was facing and the strain put on small businesses. Later in 1986 the City Council introduced legislation to regulate rent for retail spaces, citing similar hardship concerns for small businesses. Now, as our city contends with the long-lasting economic impacts of a global pandemic that hasn't been seen before in our lifetime, we are called to ask ourselves how we are committing to COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 13 change. What legacy will this administration and council leave behind for our small businesses and how will we start forward on a path for a just recovery that puts the well-being of our neighborhoods first and includes the spaces that make them so unique. Local government has the ability to do big things and today's hearing of Intro 1796 shows that. But first I'd like to be clear what this bill does not do. It does not cancel rent and it does not reduce rent. It does not guarantee any business a right to a space. It does not guarantee a right to renewal of a lease. It does not interfere with existing leases or contracts. This is what the bill does. First, Intro 1796 would create a level playing field for businesses by establish a commercial rent guidelines board, much like the residential rent guidelines board, that will annually set the maximum percentage that rents for smaller commercial spaces can be increased. It will not be a decrease. There will be a setting the maximum percentage that can be increased from the existing rent paid. The bill applies universally to all commercial spaces under a certain square footage, removing the negative incentive that landlords have to push out local COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 14 businesses and wait for the highest bidder, sometimes causing years of vacant storefronts. The interest to displace a local business is taken away because the next tenant would follow the same rental amount. New York City knows how rent stabilization works. It has given millions of households the security and stability that they needed to start a family and to be able to stay in the city. Small businesses deserve that same stability. Rent stabilization gives small businesses a fairer shot. Chain businesses and corporations have had a leg up in our city for years because it is currently in the landlord's fiscal interest to rent to well- capitalized businesses, making it harder for new businesses to get started. This goes against the interest of vibrant sustainable communities. Second, the rent guidelines board will be able to choose each year whether it will set rent increases, rent increase limits by setting one rate for the entire city or by identifying smaller affected areas. The board will be required to factor in things like building operating costs, neighborhood displacement, local economic impact, and vacancy rates, providing flexibility in a tailored approach to different needs COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 15 across the city rather than a one-size-fits-all. The bill also brings us a step closer to standardized leases so that all commercial tenants know what to expect in their rental agreements. I have seen in working on this bill wildly fluctuating leases that have snuck in unexpected costs, sometimes not until years three or four, when a tenant was least expecting it. Clearer leases are especially important coming out of the pandemic when economic instability can lead to desperation and exploitation of those most vulnerable. And so this bill eliminates the addition of pass-alongs in leases. Your total rent will actually be your total rent. New York City has the clear legal authority to enact commercial rent regulation. There is no current state law governing commercial rent and there has not been one in generations. The city has home rule authority to regulate any area of economic life where the state does not have a regulatory scheme in place. That is why this bill is legal. Intro 1796 brings regulation stability for small businesses in a time of so much instability. It creates a system of protection and reasonable rent charge, rent, rent changes, and an end to skyrocketing rent increases COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 16 and deceptive lease renewals. I want to be clear. This bill does not take aim at small landlords who are often already offering lease renewals and new leases with reasonable neighborhood market changes of 5% to 10%. It does take aim at larger corporate property holders that are gouging local businesses and causing significant displacement in our communities. Now is the time to pass this legislation, and as we start to come out of this pandemic we can offer the stability and the long-term planning that businesses have been demanding of us. Other localities are finding ways to tackle the small business rent prices. Seattle passed a law last summer to cap any commercial rent increases in response to the pandemic. When we fight for our small businesses we fight for all of us. We fight for jobs for local residents, for investment in our local economy, and the vibrancy and diversity of our neighborhoods. Our communities depend on local businesses and I'm proud to be able to put them first in this legislation. There are some folks I want to thank for this legislation. Ah, first, Kelly Taylor and Rob Newman, um, who worked on this legislation, ah, going back about three years at this point. COMMITTEE ON SMALL BUSINESS 17 Louis Holden Brown, Audrey Sun, Bill Drafter, Stephanie Jones, committee counsel. Um, I want to specifically acknowledge Elizabeth Adams, who put countless hours, um, into working through the complexity of this legislation. I just want to thank her, um, very much. Um, and all of the businesses in District 33 who helped inform this legislation, and members of the United for Small Business Coalition, who have also put in countless hours of work and advocacy. With that, I'll turn it back to you, Chair. Thank you very much for the courtesy.

Ah, thank you very much, Chair. Thank you, Commissioner. Um, I appreciate your testimony, um, and, um, and your willingness to engage with us on this topic. Um, I, I want to ask just at the outset here, um, ah, and, and Chair Gjonaj had spoken about this, um, do you hear when you're speak to small businesses out there in the city, do you hear from them that rent burden is one of the first or second top issues that they face?
Would you say it's one of the first or two, one of the first or second, ah, issues that you hear from them?

Um, has, when SBS looks at, does SBS look at the, the impact of what we call gentrification on small businesses, um, in, across the five boroughs? Is that a, is that kind of within the purview of SBS?
